paras: The murder of John Aikens was the killing of a 28-year-old Black farmer in Calvin township, Cass county, Michigan, who disappeared on the night of December 23, 1887, and whose body was recovered from a lake in early May 1888. Two young men, Lewis Wilson and Gus Harris, were jailed after Wilson confessed to a part in sinking the body. The confession drew wire coverage from Indiana to Washington, and one dispatch reported that "lynching feeling" against the accused ran high.

According to a dispatch from Vandalia, Aikens lived in a township "largely inhabited by colored people" and was popular in the Long Lake region. Elkhart dispatches described him as "a prominent young colored man" who had had trouble with the suspects at a ball.

The Vandalia account said Aikens left a shooting match very drunk, drank more at the house of Gus Harris, and was not seen again. Stories circulated of an altercation near the shore of Shave Head Lake in which his voice was identified, and it was generally believed he had been killed and put in the lake. Suspects were arrested, but with no body they were discharged.

In late April Wilson confessed; the first dispatches said he admitted that he and two others killed Aikens, hid the body in a haystack for two days, and sank it in the lake with a heavy weight. Later reports gave a different version, in which Wilson said Harris did the killing and he only helped carry the body from a barn and weight it with a bag of sand. Wilson also said Harris claimed that his stepmother, "an old flame of Aikens'," had tried to poison Aikens that day.

On the Sunday that divers searched the lake, more than 1,500 people gathered to watch. Two fishermen found the body a few days later near the house of Alexander Aikens, with marks of a heavy blow and the forehead crushed. An Elkhart report placed the body floating in Long lake with the neck broken.

An inquest was begun at Alexander Aikens's house. Wilson escaped from the officers on a Wednesday but was recaptured, and both he and Harris were held in jail; the Vandalia dispatch said more arrests were expected and that as many as five people might be involved. The Indianapolis Journal reported that Wilson's account was supposed to have been made to divert suspicion from himself. No report of an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage, and no mob is reported to have formed.

Only white papers covered the case, and they treated it as a crime and confession story rather than a racial one. The Indianapolis Journal ran the Elkhart special on April 28 under "A Murderer Confesses His Crime and Implicates Two Other Men" and printed the discovery of the body on May 5. The Washington Evening Star gave race the headline, "One of Three Colored Murderers Could Not Keep His Hideous Secret," and closed with the note that "lynching feeling runs very high," without comment.

The Maysville Evening Bulletin cut the story to a joking line among its "Pointed Paragraphs," saying the killers had "omitted to dispose of their consciences the same way." The Michigan Telegram-Herald's "A Murder Mystery" gave the fullest account, stressing the victim's good parentage and popularity and the size of the crowd at the lake.

The accounts differ on place: the Vandalia dispatch puts the killing in Calvin township, Cass county, while the Elkhart reports carry only an Indiana dateline and place it "a few miles south" of Elkhart. They also differ on the date, given as December 23, January, about three months before April 30, or "early spring," and on whether Aikens had been at a dance or a shooting match. The earlier dispatches call all three suspects colored, while the Vandalia account names only Wilson as colored and does not give Harris's race.

reader.title: Murder of John Aikens
bases: The papers describe a killing of one colored man by two or three acquaintances after a quarrel or a dispute over a woman, not a mob or band action; the only mob element is a reported 'lynching feeling' against the accused (A2, A4, A5).

An Elkhart wire dispatch (A1, A2, A3) and a separate Vandalia, Michigan dispatch (A4), with an Elkhart follow-up (A5), agree that Aikens disappeared, that Wilson confessed to a part in disposing of the body in a lake, and that the body was later found.
